q: A resting neuron's membrane potential is reported as −70 mV. What does the minus sign tell you?
options: The inside of the cell is negative compared with the outside
The outside of the cell is negative compared with the inside
The cell has lost 70 mmol/L of positive ions
The cytosol holds more negative ions than positive ions throughout

q: An experimental cell has a membrane that lets potassium through and no other ion. It starts with 140 mmol/L K+ inside and 4 mmol/L outside. Where does its membrane potential settle?
options: At 0 mV
At about −70 mV, the typical resting value
At about +60 mV
At about −90 mV

q: A typical neuron rests at −70 mV. Potassium's equilibrium potential is about −90 mV and sodium's is about +60 mV. What best explains why the resting value lies so much closer to potassium's?
options: Potassium ions are smaller and lighter than sodium ions
Far more potassium channels than sodium channels are open at rest
Each pump cycle moves more potassium ions than sodium ions
The body contains more total potassium than total sodium

q: Mr. Okafor, 62, with kidney failure, has a blood potassium of 7.1 mmol/L (normal 3.5–5.0). What happens to the resting membrane potential of his heart muscle cells?
options: It becomes more negative (hyperpolarized)
It does not change
It becomes less negative (depolarized)
It becomes positive
misconception: the potassium inside cells is what changes in hyperkalemia

q: Ms. Reyes, 48, takes a water pill that makes her kidneys lose potassium. Her blood potassium is now 2.8 mmol/L. In most of her cells, how does the resting membrane potential change?
options: It becomes more negative
It becomes less negative
It becomes positive
It does not change

q: Which of these contribute to the negative charge inside a resting cell? Select all that apply.
options: Potassium diffusing out through leak channels
Negatively charged proteins that cannot leave the cell
The pump moving 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in
Sodium diffusing in through leak channels
Water entering the cell by osmosis

q: A neuron's membrane potential moves from −70 mV to −60 mV. The inside is still negative. What is this change called?
options: Hyperpolarization
Repolarization
Depolarization
Reversal of polarity
misconception: depolarization means the inside becomes positive

q: A neuron at rest opens extra potassium channels, and its membrane potential moves from −70 mV to −78 mV. Which best explains the change?
options: More potassium enters, neutralizing negative charge inside
More potassium leaves, moving the voltage toward potassium's −90 mV
More sodium leaks in, adding positive charge inside
The pump slows, so fewer positive ions are exported

q: After a brief depolarization to +20 mV, a membrane returns to −70 mV. What is the return called?
options: Hyperpolarization
Depolarization
Equilibrium
Repolarization

q: Level 1. Extracellular potassium around a neuron rises from 4 to 8 mmol/L. Nothing else changes. Predict each variable.

variables.name: Potassium concentration gradient across the membrane
How negative potassium's equilibrium potential is
How negative the resting membrane potential is
Potassium concentration inside the cell

q: Level 4. A toxin completely blocks every sodium–potassium pump in a neuron. Predict each variable first in the first few seconds, then after several hours.

variables.name: How negative the resting potential is, in the first few seconds
Sodium concentration inside the cell, after several hours
Potassium concentration gradient, after several hours
How negative the resting potential is, after several hours

misconception: the pump creates the resting potential

q: Put the events that set up the resting membrane potential in order.
options: The pump builds high potassium inside and high sodium outside
Potassium diffuses out through open leak channels
Negative proteins left behind make the inside negative
The negative inside pulls potassium back, slowing its exit
A small sodium leak settles the voltage near −70 mV

q: One step in this account of the resting potential is wrong. Find it.
options: Potassium is about 140 mmol/L inside and about 4 mmol/L outside
Many potassium leak channels are open at rest
Sodium leaves the cell through leak channels, carrying positive charge out
The negative inside opposes further potassium exit
The voltage settles near −70 mV

q: Fill in the missing step. Potassium diffuses out through leak channels → ______ → the inside becomes negative → the negative inside pulls potassium back.
options: Trapped negative proteins stay behind
Sodium rushes in to replace the potassium
The pump moves potassium back in at the same rate
Chloride leaves the cell alongside the potassium

q: A student says: "Building a −70 mV resting potential must drain a large share of the cell's potassium." What is the best response?
options: Correct: about half of the cell's potassium leaves
Correct, which is why the pump must refill the cell after every change in voltage
Incorrect: potassium does not move at rest
Incorrect: far fewer than one potassium ion in a thousand needs to leave
misconception: building the resting potential empties the cell of potassium

q: A resting cell suddenly opens so many sodium channels that it passes sodium far more easily than potassium. Where does its membrane potential head?
options: Toward −90 mV
Toward +60 mV
Toward 0 mV and stops there
It stays at −70 mV

q: Which statement best describes the main role of the sodium–potassium pump in a resting cell?
options: It generates nearly all of the −70 mV by moving extra positive charge out
It keeps the ion gradients from running down
It opens potassium leak channels
It moves sodium into the cell

q: In the setup shown, a student accidentally swaps the electrodes: the one in the cytosol becomes the reference, and the one outside becomes the recording electrode. The cell is unchanged. What does the meter now read?
options: −70 mV
0 mV
+70 mV

fig.alt: A patch of plasma membrane with positive charges lined up along its outer face and negative charges along its inner face. A fine electrode pokes through the membrane into the cytosol, a second electrode sits in the fluid outside, and the meter joining them reads minus 70 millivolts.

q: Blood flow to part of a patient's brain stops. Within minutes, neurons in that area lose their resting potential. What is the most direct chain of events?
options: Low oxygen opens sodium leak channels, which flood the cells with sodium
Less ATP is made, so the sodium–potassium pumps slow and the ion gradients run down
Low oxygen blocks potassium leak channels, so no charge separates
Low oxygen raises the potassium concentration inside the neurons

q: Which of these are excitable cells? Select all that apply.
options: A neuron
A skeletal muscle fiber
A heart muscle cell
A red blood cell
A fibroblast in a tendon

q: A light touch depolarizes a nerve ending by 3 mV. A firmer touch at the same spot depolarizes it by 9 mV. Neither reaches threshold. What kind of change is this?
options: Two action potentials of different sizes
Graded potentials
A refractory period
Hyperpolarization

q: A stimulus depolarizes a neuron's membrane from −70 mV to −60 mV. Threshold is −55 mV. What happens next?
options: A small action potential that peaks below +30 mV
A full action potential, delayed slightly
The depolarization fades and the membrane returns to about −70 mV
The membrane stays at −60 mV until another stimulus arrives

q: A sensory nerve fiber fires action potentials that peak at +30 mV when you touch it lightly. You press twice as hard. What changes in the fiber's action potentials?
options: Each one peaks at about +60 mV
Each one lasts twice as long
They fire more times each second
They travel twice as fast
misconception: a stronger stimulus makes a bigger action potential

q: Jamal gets a lidocaine injection before a filling. Lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels in the nerve fibers of his lip and tooth. Why can he no longer feel the drill?
options: His nerve fibers can no longer produce action potentials
His nerve fibers' resting potential drops to −90 mV
His nerve endings no longer produce graded potentials
His nerve fibers become permanently refractory

q: Level 2. A toxin blocks the voltage-gated sodium channels in a nerve fiber. A stimulus is applied to the fiber's nerve ending. Predict each variable compared with before the toxin.

variables.name: Resting membrane potential
Graded potential at the nerve ending
Number of action potentials along the fiber
Peak voltage reached along the fiber

q: Put the events of an action potential in order, starting from rest.
options: A graded depolarization reaches threshold
Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium rushes in
The membrane reaches about +30 mV
Sodium channels close and potassium flows out through voltage-gated channels
The membrane dips briefly below rest
Potassium channels close and the membrane returns to rest

q: One step in this account of an action potential is wrong. Find it.
options: The membrane is depolarized to threshold
Voltage-gated sodium channels open, and sodium enters
The membrane reaches about +30 mV
The sodium–potassium pump then repolarizes the membrane
Slow-closing potassium channels cause a brief hyperpolarization
misconception: the pump repolarizes the membrane after each action potential

q: Fill in the missing step. Membrane reaches threshold → ______ → membrane rises rapidly to about +30 mV.
options: Voltage-gated potassium channels open and potassium leaves
Voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium rushes into the cell
The pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in
Leak channels close

q: On this graph, the trace climbs steeply from about −55 mV to about +30 mV. What ion movement produces that steep climb?
options: Potassium flowing out of the cell
Chloride flowing into the cell
Sodium flowing into the cell
Sodium being pumped out of the cell

fig.alt: A graph of membrane potential in millivolts against time, marked with six numbered stages. The trace sits flat at minus 70 millivolts, creeps upward after a stimulus, shoots steeply up to about plus 30 millivolts, falls back just as steeply, dips below minus 70 for a moment, and then settles back at minus 70.

q: This graph shows several depolarizing bumps of different sizes, and several hyperpolarizing dips. What does the graph show about graded potentials?
options: Only those reaching threshold trigger an action potential
They are all-or-none, just like action potentials
The hyperpolarizing dips bring the membrane closer to threshold
Longer stimuli trigger action potentials whatever their size

fig.alt: A graph of membrane potential against time with a dashed threshold line near minus 55 millivolts. On the left, upward bumps from minus 70 grow with stimulus size; a longer stimulus gives a wider bump, and only the largest bump crosses the threshold line. On the right, downward dips from minus 70 get deeper, reaching nearly minus 90 millivolts.

q: A stimulus hyperpolarizes a neuron's dendrite from −70 mV to −76 mV. A second, depolarizing stimulus of the usual size then arrives. Compared with usual, how likely is the neuron to reach threshold?
options: More likely
Less likely
Equally likely
Certain, whatever the size of the second stimulus

q: An action potential starts in the middle of an axon in a lab dish. Charge spreads in both directions from the firing patch. Why does an action potential in a living neuron, which starts near the cell body, travel only toward the axon terminals?
options: The patch just behind it has just fired and is refractory
Axons have sodium channels only on the side facing the terminals
Positive charge spreads in only one direction inside an axon
The axon terminals attract positive ions

q: A strong stimulus is applied to a neuron half a millisecond after an action potential has started. What happens?
options: A second action potential starts at once
The first action potential grows larger
No second action potential starts
The membrane hyperpolarizes immediately

q: A drug keeps the voltage-gated potassium channels of a neuron from opening. Sodium channels work normally. How does the neuron's action potential change?
options: It never reaches threshold
Its peak rises far above +60 mV
It shows a deeper dip below rest
It returns to rest more slowly

q: An action potential travels one meter from your spinal cord to your foot. How does its size at the foot compare with its size near the spinal cord?
options: Much smaller, like a graded potential
Slightly smaller
Larger
About the same

q: Two axons have no insulating wrapping. One is 10 times wider than the other. Which carries action potentials faster?
options: The wider axon
The narrower axon
Both at the same speed
Neither; axons without wrapping cannot propagate action potentials

q: Mr. Okafor, 62, has a blood potassium of 8.0 mmol/L. His muscle cells have been held partly depolarized for hours, yet his muscles are weak rather than twitchy. What best explains the weakness?
options: The depolarization has made his resting potential more negative
Many sodium channels are stuck closed
His potassium channels cannot open
The extra potassium blocks his sodium–potassium pumps

q: Which feature belongs to a graded potential but not to an action potential?
options: It can hyperpolarize without depolarizing first
It depends on voltage-gated sodium channels
It travels long distances without shrinking
It has a refractory period

q: What is a ligand?
options: A protein channel that is always open
A cell that responds to a hormone
An enzyme that breaks down chemical messengers after they are released
A molecule that binds specifically to a site on a protein

q: A hormone in the blood reaches cells in the liver, skin and fat tissue equally. Only the liver cells respond. What best explains this?
options: The hormone is broken down before reaching the skin and fat tissue
Liver cells have more ATP than skin and fat cells
Only the liver cells carry receptor proteins that bind this hormone
The hormone enters every cell equally but produces an effect only in the liver
misconception: a hormone affects every cell it reaches

q: The same neurotransmitter slows the heart rate but makes smooth muscle in the gut contract harder. How can one messenger have opposite-seeming effects?
options: It reaches the heart in a smaller amount
Heart cells and gut cells carry different receptor proteins for it
It is converted into a different molecule in the gut
Heart muscle has no receptor proteins for it, so it responds only indirectly

q: Endothelial cells lining a blood vessel release nitric oxide. It diffuses a few micrometers into the smooth muscle around the vessel, which relaxes. What kind of signaling is this?
options: Autocrine
Endocrine (hormonal)
Synaptic
Paracrine

q: An activated white blood cell releases an interleukin. The interleukin binds receptor proteins on that same white blood cell and drives it to divide. What kind of signaling is this?
options: Paracrine
Autocrine
Endocrine (hormonal)
Synaptic

q: Leo, 30, takes ibuprofen for a sprained ankle for two weeks. The pain and swelling ease, but he develops stomach pain. Which explanation fits both effects?
options: Ibuprofen blocks the receptor proteins for neurotransmitters in both the injured ankle and the lining of the stomach
Ibuprofen raises cAMP in every cell
Less prostaglandin is made, so fewer pain endings are sensitized and the stomach lining is less protected
Ibuprofen kills white blood cells in the ankle and stomach

q: A newly discovered messenger is a small, hydrophobic molecule made from cholesterol. Where are its receptor proteins most likely to be?
options: Inside the target cell, in the cytosol or nucleus
In the plasma membrane, facing out
In the blood plasma
On the outer surface of the nuclear envelope, facing the cytosol

q: Priya's reliever inhaler opens her airways within minutes. A steroid tablet she takes for the same problem needs several hours to work, and its effect lasts much longer. What best explains the difference?
options: The tablet is absorbed slowly from the gut, and slow absorption accounts for both its late start and its long effect
The inhaler acts through a surface receptor protein and cAMP; the steroid changes gene expression
The steroid acts on a different organ from the one the inhaled drug reaches in the airways
The inhaled drug is more concentrated

q: Put the steps of a G-protein-coupled receptor pathway in order.
options: The first messenger binds a receptor protein in the membrane
The receptor protein switches on a G protein
The G protein switches on a membrane enzyme
The enzyme converts ATP into cAMP
cAMP switches on enzymes that phosphorylate target proteins
The phosphorylated proteins change the cell's activity

q: One step in this account of a water-soluble messenger's action is wrong. Find it.
options: The messenger travels dissolved in the plasma
It crosses the plasma membrane and binds a receptor protein in the nucleus
A G protein is switched on
cAMP is made from ATP
Enzymes switched on by cAMP phosphorylate target proteins

q: Fill in the missing step at a synapse. Action potential reaches the axon terminal → voltage-gated calcium channels open and calcium enters → ______ → neurotransmitter binds receptor proteins on the postsynaptic cell.
options: The action potential jumps across the synaptic cleft
The postsynaptic cell releases calcium into the cleft
Vesicles fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis
Neurotransmitter is made from ATP in the cleft

q: Level 2. A drug blocks the enzyme that breaks down cAMP in heart muscle cells. A messenger that raises cAMP in these cells then binds its receptor protein as usual. Predict each variable compared with no drug.

variables.name: Number of receptor proteins occupied by the messenger
cAMP concentration inside the cells
Phosphorylation of the target proteins
How long the response lasts after the messenger leaves

q: A hormone present in the blood at less than a billionth of a mole per liter causes a large response in its target cells. What best explains how so little hormone can do so much?
options: Each hormone molecule binds thousands of receptor proteins at once
Each step of the second messenger pathway multiplies the signal many times
The hormone is converted into ATP inside the cell
Target cells concentrate the hormone a millionfold before responding

q: During a bad month, Priya uses her reliever inhaler many times a day. Each puff opens her airways less than before, even though the dose is the same. Which change in her airway muscle cells best explains this?
options: Up-regulation of the drug's receptor proteins
The drug's receptor proteins moved into the nucleus
Down-regulation of the drug's receptor proteins
Her airway muscle stopped making ATP

q: The nerve to a skeletal muscle is cut. Weeks later, the muscle fibers respond strongly to even tiny amounts of the nerve's neurotransmitter applied anywhere on their surface. What happened?
options: The fibers up-regulated receptor proteins for that neurotransmitter
The fibers down-regulated receptor proteins for that neurotransmitter
The neurotransmitter became lipid-soluble
The fibers became autocrine cells

q: Which statements are true of lipid-soluble messengers such as steroids? Select all that apply.
options: They diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer
They bind intracellular receptors
They mostly change gene expression
They usually act within milliseconds
They travel in blood mostly bound to proteins that carry them

q: You touch a hot pan and pull your hand away in a fraction of a second. Why is this response carried by the nervous system rather than by a hormone?
options: Hormones cannot reach the arm
Hormones only affect organs, not muscles
Neurotransmitters travel through the blood to the arm muscles much faster than hormones do
Nerve signals reach specific muscles in milliseconds; hormones take seconds or more

q: In the pathway shown, a mutation leaves the G protein unable to be switched on. The first messenger still binds its receptor protein normally. What happens?
options: cAMP rises, and the cell responds
The receptor protein makes cAMP directly, and the cell responds normally
The messenger enters the cell instead
No cAMP is made, and the cell does not respond

fig.alt: A water-soluble messenger stays outside the cell and binds a protein in the plasma membrane. That protein switches on a G protein on the inner face, which switches on a membrane enzyme that turns ATP into cyclic AMP. Cyclic AMP then switches on enzymes that attach phosphate groups to other proteins in the cytoplasm, changing what the cell does.

q: At the synapse shown, a drug occupies the receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane without opening them. The presynaptic cell fires normally. What is the result?
options: Neurotransmitter is released normally, but the postsynaptic cell barely responds
No neurotransmitter is released
The postsynaptic cell fires more often
The presynaptic cell's action potential stops before reaching the terminal

fig.alt: A small drawing of a neuron has a box around one point on its surface, and an arrow leads to an enlarged view of that point. In the enlarged view, the swollen end of an axon from another neuron sits close to the receiving neuron's membrane without touching it: a narrow gap separates them. Small membrane sacs inside the axon ending fuse with its membrane and release molecules that cross the gap and bind channel proteins in the receiving neuron's membrane.

q: Which phrase describes a receptor protein rather than a sensory receptor?
options: A nerve ending in the skin that detects pressure on the surface
A cell in the eye that detects light
A protein that binds a specific chemical messenger
A nerve ending that detects heat

q: Which feature defines a gland as exocrine?
options: It releases enzymes rather than hormones
Its product leaves through a duct
It is built from connective tissue
It has a dense network of capillaries
misconception: glands are classified by the chemical they make

q: Under the microscope, a cluster of epithelial cells sits wrapped in capillaries. You find no duct anywhere near it, and the cells are full of secretory vesicles. What kind of gland is this most likely to be?
options: A simple tubular exocrine gland
A mucous gland
An endocrine gland
A unicellular exocrine gland

q: Mrs. Lee, 62, has a tumor pressing on the main duct of her pancreas. Her stools become greasy because she no longer digests fat well. Her blood levels of the hormones her pancreas makes stay normal. Which explanation fits both findings?
options: The tumor destroyed the hormone-making cells first
Enzymes and hormones share the same duct
The tumor made hormones that replaced lost ones
Enzymes need the duct; hormones go straight into the blood

q: A goblet cell in the lining of your airway releases mucus directly onto the surface. How is a goblet cell classified?
options: A unicellular exocrine gland
A unicellular endocrine gland
A compound mucous gland
A holocrine gland

q: A gland has a duct that divides again and again, like the branches of a tree. Each smallest branch ends in a rounded sac of secretory cells. What is this gland's name?
options: Simple tubular
Simple alveolar
Compound alveolar
Compound tubuloalveolar

q: In a gland, cells near the base are small and dividing. Cells farther in are larger and packed with lipid. At the center, cells are breaking apart, and their fragments are part of the fluid the gland releases. Which mode of secretion is this?
options: Merocrine
Holocrine
Apocrine
Endocrine

q: A drug stops mitosis in the stem cells at the base of a holocrine gland for two weeks. Predict each variable at the end of that time.

variables.name: Number of new secretory cells produced in the gland
Amount of secretion the gland releases
Output of a nearby merocrine gland whose cells are not dividing

q: Select every statement that is true of endocrine glands.
options: They have no duct.
Their product enters interstitial fluid and then the blood.
Their product changes the cells that carry a matching receptor protein.
Their product is carried to the inside of the gut through a duct.
They consist of a single cell.

q: Put the steps in order for an enzyme-making cell of the pancreas releasing its protein product.
options: Ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum build the protein.
The Golgi apparatus modifies the protein and packs it into secretory vesicles.
The vesicles move to the apical surface of the cell.
Each vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and empties its contents by exocytosis.
The product enters the lumen of the duct.
The duct carries the product to the inside of the gut.

q: Fill the gap. A pituitary gland cell releases its hormone by exocytosis → ______ → the hormone enters a capillary → the blood carries it through the body → it binds a receptor protein on a target cell.
options: The hormone diffuses through the interstitial fluid
The hormone flows through a duct
The hormone lands on the skin surface
The hormone binds a receptor protein on the gland cell itself

q: This pathway for a compound alveolar exocrine gland contains one wrong step. Find it.
options: Secretory cells in the sacs make an enzyme.
Vesicles release the enzyme into the lumen of the sac by exocytosis.
The enzyme diffuses into capillaries around the sac.
Small ducts join into larger ducts.
The main duct empties the enzyme onto the lining of the gut.

q: A student says: "If a gland makes an enzyme it is exocrine, and if it makes a hormone it is endocrine." To decide the type of a gland you have never seen before, which observation settles it?
options: Whether the product is a protein
Whether the cells store their product in secretory vesicles
Whether the product leaves through a duct or passes into the blood
Whether the gland is larger than a single cell
misconception: glands are classified by the chemical they make

q: A gland's cells are packed with vesicles of protein, and the gland releases a thin, watery fluid rich in enzymes. What kind of exocrine gland is it?
options: A mucous gland
A serous gland
A holocrine gland
A ductless gland

q: Which is the clearest example of true apocrine secretion in the human body?
options: A goblet cell releasing mucus
The oil glands of the skin releasing their oily product
The thyroid gland releasing its hormone
Milk-making cells of the breast releasing droplets of milk fat
misconception: apocrine sweat glands are the model of apocrine secretion

q: What happens to a merocrine gland cell after it releases its product?
options: It stays whole and goes on making and releasing more product
Its apical part pinches off with the product
It breaks apart and becomes part of the secretion
It divides by mitosis to replace itself

q: Cells in a tissue release a chemical that diffuses a few micrometers to their neighbors and changes them. The chemical never enters the blood. How is this release best classified?
options: Endocrine signaling
Paracrine signaling
Exocrine secretion
Holocrine secretion

q: Which description matches apocrine secretion?
options: Vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and the cell stays whole
The product-filled apical end of the cell pinches off
The entire cell fills with product and breaks apart
The product diffuses from the cell into nearby capillaries

q: Which tissue membrane has no epithelium?
options: Mucous membrane
Serous membrane
Synovial membrane
Cutaneous membrane

q: A biopsy comes from the lining of a tube that opens to the outside of the body. It shows simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, resting on loose connective tissue full of capillaries and white blood cells. Which membrane is this?
options: A serous membrane
The cutaneous membrane
A synovial membrane
A mucous membrane

q: A surgeon takes a sample of the shiny membrane covering the stomach's outer surface, inside the abdominal cavity. The surface cells are thin and flat, in a single layer. Which membrane is this, and what does it release?
options: A mucous membrane releasing mucus
A serous membrane releasing serous fluid
A synovial membrane releasing joint fluid
A mucous membrane releasing serous fluid

q: Select every membrane that is an epithelial membrane.
options: Mucous membrane
Serous membrane
Cutaneous membrane
Synovial membrane
Plasma membrane

q: An hour after a bee sting, the skin around it is puffy. Which change directly causes the puffiness?
options: Vasoconstriction of the small arteries nearby
Fibroblasts laying down collagen at the site
Leakier small vessels letting fluid out into the tissue
Mast cells dividing rapidly at the site

q: Before a small skin injury, a person takes a drug that blocks the receptor proteins histamine binds to. It does not change how much histamine mast cells release. Predict each variable at the injury site, compared with the same injury without the drug.

variables.name: Amount of histamine released by mast cells
Blood flow into the area
Swelling

q: Put the steps of tissue repair after a deep cut in order.
options: Blood vessels break and a blood clot stops the bleeding.
Mast cells and damaged cells release histamine and other chemical messengers.
Vasodilation and leaky capillaries make the area red, warm and swollen.
Macrophages engulf dead cells and debris by phagocytosis.
New capillaries grow in and fibroblasts lay down collagen.
Surviving cells regenerate the surface, and collagen deep in the gap becomes scar tissue.

q: Mr. Adams, 66, had part of his heart muscle die when an artery feeding it was blocked. Months later, an ultrasound shows that part of the heart wall is thin and does not move when the rest of the heart beats. Which best explains this?
options: Scar tissue has replaced the dead heart muscle
The dead muscle regenerated but is still immature
Inflammation is still going on in that part of the wall
Apoptosis removed the cells without any repair

q: After surgery removes a large part of the liver, the liver regrows much of its lost mass. After the same amount of heart muscle dies, the heart forms a scar. What difference between the two tissues best explains this?
options: Mature liver cells can return to the cell cycle and divide
Liver has a richer blood supply than the heart
Heart muscle has no fibroblasts to lay down collagen
Liver damage sets off no inflammation at all

q: In a tissue sample, a patch of cells has swollen, their plasma membranes have ruptured, and white blood cells crowd the area around them. How did these cells most likely die?
options: Apoptosis
Mitosis
Regeneration
Necrosis

q: Why does apoptosis not set off inflammation, when necrosis does?
options: Apoptotic cells release extra histamine
It occurs in tissues without blood vessels
Its contents stay sealed until macrophages engulf them
Necrotic cells shrink and are engulfed whole

q: This explanation of the signs of inflammation contains one wrong step. Find it.
options: Injury makes mast cells release histamine by exocytosis.
Histamine causes vasoconstriction of the small arteries feeding the area.
Histamine opens gaps between endothelial cells of capillaries and the smallest veins.
Water and proteins leak into the interstitial fluid, and the tissue swells.
Chemical messengers and pressure from swelling stimulate pain-sensing nerve endings.

q: Fill the gap. Mast cells release histamine → ______ → more warm blood flows into the area → the skin looks red and feels warm.
options: Nearby small arteries dilate
Fibroblasts lay down collagen
The capillaries clot and seal shut
Macrophages engulf all the debris

q: A child gets a shallow scrape on one knee and a deep, gaping cut on the other. Which injury is more likely to heal without a visible scar, and what makes the difference?
options: The deep cut: it forms a larger clot
The scrape: its framework survives
Both heal alike: skin regenerates well
Neither: skin injuries all heal by fibrosis

q: What is the parenchyma of an organ?
options: Its supporting connective tissue framework
Its outer serous covering
Its working cells, such as liver cells
The scar tissue that forms after injury

q: A patient's knee is swollen. A needle drawn into the space inside the knee returns a large volume of thick, slippery fluid. Which membrane made this fluid, and what is it made of?
options: A serous membrane made of simple squamous epithelium
A mucous membrane made of epithelium and lamina propria
A synovial membrane made of connective tissue
The cutaneous membrane made of epidermis and dermis

q: Which feature sets the cutaneous membrane apart from the other two epithelial membranes?
options: Its surface layer is dry and keratinized
It rests on a layer of connective tissue
It covers or lines a surface of your body
Its epithelium has more than one layer of cells

q: A person's liver is injured again and again over many years by heavy drinking. Each injury is followed by repair. Predict each variable after years of this, compared with a healthy liver.

variables.name: Amount of collagen in the liver
Number of working liver cells (parenchyma)
The liver's ability to do its jobs

q: What is a set point?
options: The highest value a regulated variable can safely reach
The target value a loop holds a variable near
The point at which a positive feedback loop ends
The place in the body where a sensory receptor sits

q: A stimulus has just changed a regulated variable. Put the remaining parts of the feedback loop in the order the signal travels.
options: Sensory receptor (sensor)
Afferent pathway
Control center
Efferent pathway
Effector
Response

q: You walk into a cold room. Nerve signals from your brain make the smooth muscle in the walls of your skin's blood vessels contract, and less warm blood reaches your skin. In this loop, what is the effector?
options: The cold air of the room
The nerves carrying signals from the brain
Smooth muscle in the walls of the skin's blood vessels
The temperature control center in the brain

q: Cold-sensitive nerve endings in your skin fire action potentials that travel along sensory nerves to your brain. In the feedback loop, what are those sensory nerves?
options: The efferent pathway
The control center
The afferent pathway
The effector

q: During a run, your body temperature rises above its set point. Predict how each variable changes as your temperature control loop responds.

variables.name: Diameter of the blood vessels in your skin
Amount of sweat released onto your skin
Heat lost from your skin to the air

q: In a patient, the nerves that carry commands from the brain to the blood vessels of the skin have been damaged, so those vessels can no longer constrict. The patient sits in a cold room for an hour. Compared with a person whose loop is intact, predict each variable.

variables.name: Blood flow to the skin
Heat lost through the skin
Body temperature after an hour
